content: This experiment pitted expert pruning (REAP 512→320) against aggressive quantization (IQ1_S) on a 512-expert MoE, with a dense Qwen3.8-27B Q6_K model as a size-matched baseline. The headline result: at roughly matched model size, quantizing all 512 experts to 1-bit (67.6 GiB) beats pruning to 320 experts at Q3 (64.2 GiB) on knowledge probes by 22.8 percentage points (p = 1e-30). The pruned arms, by contrast, drop raw knowledge accuracy from 55% to roughly 35%, and about half of every committed answer becomes a fabrication rather than a refusal (refusal rates stay under 2%). A secondary hypothesis—that pruning would trade knowledge for code ability—failed: HumanEval+ scores are statistically indistinguishable between the 1-bit unpruned model (93.9%) and the pruned Q3 model (92.7%, p = 0.77). In short, if you're squeezing a MoE to fit on your hardware, quantizing the full expert set outperforms dropping experts on factual recall while matching it on code, and the pruned model's failure mode is confident hallucination rather than abstention.

content: A preregistered experiment compared MTP on versus off across 120 item-seeds. The pooled pass rate dropped from 75.0% to 69.2% (mean d = −5.8 pp, 95% CI [−12.2, +0.5], exact sign-flip p = 0.12). The preregistered equivalence test at ±10 pp was not met and harm was not detected at α = .05, making the registered verdict inconclusive. A secondary noise-floor rule (−4.4 pp) would have passed the ±10 pp TOST, but the primary rule governs. No timeouts occurred in either arm. Descriptively, MTP altered the execution trajectory in 119 of 120 runs, yet 85% of those changes left the outcome unchanged. The 12.5% of runs whose outcome flipped ran 11-to-4 against MTP, with 9 of the 11 losses labeled WRONG-ACTION. MTP was also less consistent across seeds (23.7% within-run disagreement versus 17.2% for MTP-off). The deployment reading is that the risk lies in irreversible wrong actions rather than speed, and that for retryable, verifiable work the correct metric is expected time to success, where MTP's decode speed likely wins.

Arm A scored 82.8%; arm B scored 79.3%. That 10.3% discordance is exactly the rate a Q6_K quant produced against a 3.5-bpw AD-IQ3_S quant in a prior v4 re-run (also 3/29, with a near-symmetric b:c split). Three arms of the same Q6_K file showed a 10.4-point spread in aggregate pass rates. The author concludes that every quant-comparison result from the campaign—13.9%, 12.1%, 22.2%, 27.6%, 10.3%—was measured at or below this noise floor and is therefore void, not merely underpowered. The limitation is attributed to the one-rep, temperature-1.0 configuration, not to the corpus, which was validated independently.

# VBR full-reset at chunk boundary cascades into immediate mass-degrade despite ample free VRAM

## Summary

On a ROCm build (commit `38ada0e1b`, RX 9070 XT serving as both compute and display GPU), running `llama-perplexity` with VBR KV-cache quantisation and `--chunks 2` triggers a **VBR full reset** at the chunk-1 → chunk-2 boundary. In the same millisecond the reset, a cascade of degrades (#1…#N) fires at **0 cells**, walking every KV tensor down to `turbo1_tcq` before a single token of chunk 2 has been processed. Free VRAM never dropped below 3 903 MiB during the run, so the cascade is not driven by actual memory pressure.

## Reproduction

```bash
HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 llama-perplexity \
  -m Qwen_Qwen3.5-9B-Q8_0.gguf \
  -f wiki.test.raw \
  -ngl 99 -fa on \
  -c 32768 -b 512 -ub 512 \
  -v --chunks 2 \
  -ctk vbr -ctv vbr \
  --vbr-vram 2048M
```

Environment: ROCm build, commit `38ada0e1b`, single RX 9070 XT (also the desktop display GPU).

## Observed behaviour

1. **Chunk 1** runs normally. The first VBR degrade occurs at 25 088 cells. At the end of chunk 1 the log reads:

   > `projected 552.00 / budget 2048.00 MiB (mapped 574.50) at 32768 cells`

2. **Chunk boundary:** the log immediately prints

   > `VBR full reset: cache empty -- 15 tensors back at their entry tier`

   (The model has 16 KV tensors: 8 layers × K/V.)

3. **Same millisecond**, degrades #1…#N fire at **0 cells** and walk every tensor to `turbo1_tcq` before chunk 2 has processed any tokens.

4. **Quality impact:** mean KLD vs. f16 from chunk 2 onward is ≈ 0.13, compared to 0.0022 for static q8_0 at the same context.

## Expected behaviour

- A projected usage of 552 MiB against a 2048 MiB budget should not trigger a full reset.
- Even if a reset occurs, the subsequent degrade cascade should not fire at 0 cells with thousands of MiB of VRAM still free.
- KV tensors should not be driven to `turbo1_tcq` before any new tokens are processed.

## Ruled out / mitigations

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| `VBR_FREEZE=1 VBR_BUDGET_MIB=2048` (unfrozen → frozen) | **0 degrades** across 9 chunks |
| `--vbr-vram 288M` (unfrozen) | Never triggers the cascade |
| `--vbr-vram 544M / 768M / 2048M` (unfrozen) | All end on the same floor from chunk 2 (i.e. the cascade still occurs, just at a lower tier) |
| Free-VRAM sampling (0.5 s interval) | Never below **3 903 MiB** – rules out genuine OOM as the trigger |

**Not yet tested:** behaviour under `llama-server`.

## Questions for the maintainer

- Why does the chunk-boundary reset report **15** tensors back at entry tier when the model has **16** KV tensors?
- Is the 0-cell degrade cascade a consequence of the reset re-evaluating the entire cache at the new (empty) state, or is it a separate scheduling bug?
- Should a projected-usage value well under budget (552 / 2048 MiB) be eligible for a full reset at all?

qwen3-coder parser misroutes MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B tool calls: hardcoded `"\n</parameter>\n"` delimiter does not match compactly-rendered template output

## Summary

`chat.cpp` (line 1213) selects the tool-call parser by substring-matching the chat-template **source** for `<tool_call>`, `<function=`, and `<parameter=`. The MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B Q8_0 template contains all three substrings, so requests are routed to the qwen3-coder parser. That parser, however, hardcodes the literal `"\n</parameter>\n"` as the parameter delimiter, whereas MiMo's template renders parameters compactly (no surrounding newlines). The mismatch corrupts tool-call arguments on a large fraction of multi-call turns.

## Reproduction steps

1. Load **MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B** (Q8_0) on the `llama.cpp` server.
2. Use the model's stock chat template, which emits tool calls in the form:
   ```
   <tool_call><function=NAME><parameter=KEY>value</parameter>...
   ```
   (note: no newline before or after `</parameter>`).
3. Send a prompt that elicits a multi-tool-call response.
4. Inspect the parsed arguments returned by the server.

## Observed behaviour

- **6 of 10** multi-call turns produced corrupted tool-call arguments.
- In a larger 30-turn run, **17 of 30** turns were corrupted.

## Expected behaviour

All tool-call arguments are parsed correctly (0 corrupted turns).

- **Model-side / rendering issue.** A template-level workaround—splitting the literal in the template source as `'<param' ~ 'eter='` so the substring check on line 1213 fails and the generic auto-parser is used—produces **byte-identical rendered output** yet eliminates the corruption entirely: **17/30 → 0/30** (p = 6.2 × 10⁻⁷). - Upstream issue [llama.cpp#26763](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/26763) reported a similar parser-mismatch scenario and was closed as "not a bug." The present case is distinct in that the template genuinely contains the three trigger substrings while the *rendered* delimiter differs from what the matched parser expects.

## Summary

With Open WebUI v0.11.4 (Docker) pointed at a single `llama-server` (buun, Qwen3.5-9B Q8_0) started with `-np 1`, every chat turn triggers three additional requests after the reply (follow-up suggestions, chat title, and chat tags — ~296, 628, and 574 prompt tokens respectively). Because there is only one slot, these side requests evict the reusable context checkpoint, so the next user turn is a full reprocess. The server log reports:

> full reprocess: no reusable context checkpoint

Running the same server with `-np 2` avoids the problem: the side request occupies a second slot and the main-chat context survives.

## Reproduction steps

1. Start `llama-server` (buun, Qwen3.5-9B Q8_0) with `-np 1`.
2. Point Open WebUI v0.11.4 (Docker) at that server.
3. Send a one-line question in a new chat.
   - Note the main request carries **6,411 prompt tokens** (built-in tool definitions + system prompt).
4. Wait for the reply, then observe the three follow-up requests (suggestions, title, tags).
5. Send a second message in the same chat.
   - Check the server log for `cache_n` / `prompt_n` on that request.
6. (Controlled test) Repeat steps 3–5, but after turn 2 issue one unrelated side request, then send turn 3.
7. Repeat the whole test with `-np 2` for comparison.

## Observed behaviour

| Scenario | Turn | `cache_n` | `prompt_n` | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `-np 1`, normal chat | 2 | **0** | 6,791 | Full reprocess; no cache reuse at all. |
| `-np 1`, controlled test | 2 | 2,423 | — | Cache hit (no side request yet). |
| `-np 1`, controlled test | 3 (after 1 side request) | **0** | — | Cache destroyed by the side request. |
| `-np 2`, controlled test | 3 (after 1 side request) | 2,438 | — | Cache survives; side request uses slot 2. |

Server log for the failing cases: `full reprocess: no reusable context checkpoint`.

## Expected behaviour

- The KV cache for the ongoing chat conversation should persist across turns so that the next user message only pays for the new tokens, not a full reprocess of the system prompt, tool definitions, and prior history.
- The three post-reply side requests (suggestions, title, tags) should not evict the main conversation's context checkpoint.

## Ruled out / notes

- The issue is **not** present with `-np 2`; the side request simply uses a second slot and the main-chat cache is preserved (turn 3 reuses 2,438 tokens).
- The large base prompt (6,411 tokens for a one-line question) is due to built-in tool definitions and the system prompt bundled by Open WebUI, not a misconfiguration on the llama-server side.
- The problem is reproducible with a single unrelated side request between turns; it is not an accumulation or timeout issue.

## Title

`ledger_extract.py` records compound-command output as a bare `ERR` line without the producing command, causing the diary model to fabricate a false narrative

## Summary

`tools/ledger_extract.py` records every `tool_result` with `is_error=true` as `ERR <first 120 chars>` and omits the command that produced the output. When a compound shell command exits non-zero because of its *last* sub-command, the output of an *earlier* sub-command is mislabelled as the error. That truncated, command-less string is then handed to the local model in `tools/ledger_build.py`, which invents a plausible-sounding but entirely false dev-diary entry.

## Reproduction steps

1. Execute a compound shell command of the form:
   ```
   grep … argus/driver.py …; which faketime
   ```
   where the final sub-command (`which faketime`) exits 1 because nothing matched.
2. The resulting `tool_result` is flagged `is_error=true`.
3. `ledger_extract.py` serialises it as `ERR <first 120 chars>` — in this case the grep output, an old docstring on `argus/driver.py` line 9 — with no record of which command produced it.
4. `ledger_build.py` feeds that line to the local model for the 2026-09-23 diary entry.
5. The model emits the diary text (see Observed below).

## Observed behaviour

The 2026-09-23 diary entry states:

> argus/driver.py:9 hit a route that exists in no Hermes codebase … Worked around by setting both TZ and HERMES_TIMEZONE

Neither half of that statement is true. The "route" reference is a hallucination built from the old docstring fragment; the TZ/HERMES_TIMEZONE change was unrelated to the command in question and was later found to be a bug in its own right.

## Expected behaviour

- The `ERR` record should include the command (or at least the sub-command) that produced the output, so the downstream model can attribute the text correctly.
- Because the exit status of a compound command is that of its **last** command, a non-zero exit should not cause output from earlier sub-commands to be labelled as the error. The extractor should either (a) record the full compound command alongside the output, or (b) only flag the specific sub-command whose exit status is non-zero.

## Ruled out

- **The TZ / HERMES_TIMEZONE change was not the cause or fix.** It was unrelated to the `argus/driver.py` grep and was independently identified as a bug.

## `signflip_p(ds)`

Compute a permutation-test p-value by randomly flipping the signs of the non-zero observations and measuring how often the resulting absolute mean is at least as large as the observed absolute mean. The test answers: *is the sample mean significantly different from zero under the null hypothesis that the mean is zero?*

### Parameters

| Name | Type | Description |
|------|------|-------------|
| `ds` | `Sequence[float]` | A non-empty sequence of numeric observations. |

### Returns

`tuple[float, str]`

- **p-value** – A float in \[0, 1\]. Smaller values indicate stronger evidence against a zero mean.
- **method** – `"exact"` if the sign-flip space was enumerated in full, or `"monte-carlo 1e6"` if a stochastic approximation was used.

### Method selection

Let `nz` be the subset of `ds` whose elements satisfy `abs(x) > 1e-12`.

- **Exact** (`len(nz) ≤ 22`): Enumerates all 2^len(nz) sign assignments via `itertools.product`. The p-value is `cnt / 2**len(nz)`.
- **Monte Carlo** (`len(nz) > 22`): Draws 1 000 000 random sign assignments from a `random.Random(0)` instance (deterministic across calls). The p-value is `(cnt + 1) / (n + 1)`, an add-one correction that prevents a return of exactly 0.

In both branches the statistic compared is `abs(mean of (sign × nz element) over all of ds)`, i.e. the denominator is always `len(ds)`, not `len(nz)`.

### Edge cases

- **Empty `ds`** – Raises `ZeroDivisionError` at `sum(ds) / len(ds)`. The caller must guard against this.
- **All values ≈ 0** (`len(nz) == 0`) – The exact path runs with `repeat=0` (one empty sign vector). The p-value will be `1.0` because the observed statistic is also ~0.
- **p-value of 0 (exact path)** – Possible when no sign assignment reaches the observed magnitude. The Monte Carlo path cannot return 0 due to the `+1` correction (minimum ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁶).
- **Floating-point tolerance** – The comparison threshold is `obs - 1e-12`, a small relaxation to absorb rounding error in the sign-flip sums.
- **Reproducibility** – The Monte Carlo branch is fully deterministic (fixed seed 0). The exact branch is trivially deterministic.
- **Dependencies** – Requires `itertools` and `random` to be in scope (imported at module level).

## `annotate_unverified(entry, ev)`

### Purpose

Post-hoc mechanical guard that flags sentences in a diary entry which *assert* an error, failure, or causal explanation while naming an identifier that is **not** backed by a genuine tool failure in the accompanying event log. The tag is appended inline; the original sentence is never removed or altered, so a claim the check cannot see still survives for a human reader.

Added 2026-09-24 in response to a 09-23 entry that fabricated a root cause from a `grep` that matched nothing.

### Inputs

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `entry` | `str` | The full diary-entry text (may span multiple lines). |
| `ev` | `list[tuple[str, str]]` | Event-log records as `(key, value)` pairs. Only records whose key is `"ERR"` are inspected. A value beginning with `"[NONZERO]"` denotes a search/command that exited non-zero **without producing a matching error line** (i.e. it "found nothing"); any other `"ERR"` value is treated as a genuine failure. |

### Outputs

Returns a **tuple**:

| Element | Type | Description |
|---------|------|-------------|
| `annotated_text` | `str` | The original entry with zero or more inline tags of the form ` _[unverified: \`<id>\` <reason>]_` appended to the end of the offending sentence (after trailing whitespace is stripped). |
| `tagged` | `int` | Number of sentences that received a tag. |

### How a sentence is (or is not) tagged

A sentence is tagged only when **all** of the following hold:

1. It matches the module-level `CLAIM_WORDS` regex (i.e. it asserts an error, failure, or cause).
2. It does **not** already contain the substring `_[unverified` (idempotency guard).
3. It contains at least one identifier (extracted via `IDENT.findall`, taking the first or second capture group, filtered to length ≥ 3).
4. **None** of those identifiers appear in the "real" failure text (the concatenation of all non-`[NONZERO]` `ERR` values).

Given those four conditions, the tag reason is chosen as:

* **"appears only in a search that found nothing, not in a failure"** – the identifier *does* appear in the `[NONZERO]` search output.
* **"no tool failure in this window mentions it"** – the identifier appears in neither `real` nor `nonzero`, **and** the sentence is inside an *error narrative* (see below) **and** either matches `CAUSAL` or starts with an "error" heading pattern.

If the identifier is absent from both `real` and `nonzero` but the sentence is **not** in an error narrative, it is left untagged (treated as a plain mention of a failure elsewhere, e.g. the system under test).

### Error-narrative context

`context["error_para"]` is a per-line flag that governs whether the "no tool failure" branch is reachable:

* Set to `True` at the start of a line if the line matches `^\s*(- )?\*\*error` (case-insensitive) — i.e. the line opens an `**Error**` paragraph or a bulleted variant.
* Set to `True` mid-line as soon as **any** sentence in that line receives a tag, so subsequent sentences in the same paragraph are also scrutinised under the stricter rule.
* Reset to `False` at the top of each new line.

### Sentence splitting

Within each line, sentences are split with:

```
re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z*`_])", line)
```

This splits on whitespace that follows `.`, `!`, or `?` **and** is followed by an uppercase letter, `*`, backtick, or underscore. Sentences that begin with a lowercase letter or other characters are **not** split from the preceding text and will be evaluated as part of the previous chunk.

### Edge cases & behavioural notes

* **Idempotent.** Running the function on already-annotated text will not double-tag, because any sentence containing `_[unverified` is skipped.
* **Short identifiers ignored.** Identifiers with fewer than 3 characters are discarded before the match check, so a 1- or 2-character token in the sentence will not trigger a tag.
* **Only the first identifier is named in the tag.** If a sentence contains multiple unverified identifiers, `ids[0]` is the one shown; the others are not listed.
* **Trailing whitespace.** The tag is appended to `sent.rstrip()`, so any trailing spaces/tabs on the original sentence are removed before the tag is added.
* **No deletion, no reordering.** The function returns the text with the same line structure (`"\n".join`); no line is dropped, merged, or reordered.
* **`ev` keys other than `"ERR"`** are silently ignored.
* **Module-level regexes.** `CLAIM_WORDS`, `IDENT`, and `CAUSAL` are expected to be compiled `re.Pattern` objects defined elsewhere in the module; they are not parameters.
* **The "window" is the entire `ev` list.** There is no temporal or positional filtering of log entries; every `ERR` record in `ev` is in scope for the check.

**KV-cache quantization** compresses the key/value tensors you accumulate per token during autoregressive decoding. Normally stored in fp16/bf16, you round them to int8, int4, or mixed precisions. The motivation is memory: a 70B model at 8k context can eat 30–60 GB of KV cache alone, which dominates your VRAM budget and caps how long you can run.

Second, you pay a dequantize-on-read (or quantize-on-write) op per attention step. In practice inference is memory-bandwidth-bound, so moving fewer bytes more than offsets the extra ALU work, and net latency improves.

A variable-bit-rate scheme allocates bits *non-uniformly*—e.g., per-token, per-channel, or per-head. Heuristics might give earlier positions or high-magnitude channels 8 bits and the rest 4, or use a learned/per-tensor scale. The payoff: at the same average memory you get closer-to-fp16 quality, or at the same quality you shrink the cache further. The cost is bookkeeping (variable-length layouts, per-block scales) and slightly more complex kernel code. Think of it as moving from a flat allocation to an entropy-coded one.

Speculative decoding is a *rejection-sampling* trick, not a new model. The draft head (MTP or otherwise) proposes *k* tokens; the target model then runs one parallel forward pass and re-scores every position with its own full distribution. Each proposed token is accepted with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft) and, on rejection, you resample from the truncated-and-renormalized residual (p_target − p_draft)⁺. That residual is provably a valid sample from p_target, so the marginal distribution over output sequences is mathematically identical to plain autoregressive decoding.

In practice, outputs can still drift for a few reasons:

- **Floating-point re-association.** The parallel verification pass groups GEMMs, attention softmaxes, and reductions differently than the sequential loop. Logits shift by ~1e-7, which after softmax can flip an argmax or nudge a token across a top-k / top-p boundary.
- **RNG state divergence.** The draft forward pass (and any extra kernels) consume or reorder CUDA RNG draws, so even sampling from an identical distribution lands on a different token.
- **Nucleus/top-k cutoffs.** A 1e-7 logit shift right at the cumulative-probability threshold changes which tokens enter the candidate set, altering the conditional distribution you actually sample from.

None of these violate the theory; they're the usual non-determinism of GPU inference amplified by a different computation graph.

The router (a small linear layer + softmax) runs on the GPU and, for each token, selects *k* experts out of *N*. If expert weights don't fit in VRAM, you keep some in system RAM. At inference time the forward pass forks: tokens routed to GPU-resident experts proceed in the normal tensor-core pipeline, while tokens routed to RAM-resident experts require a device-to-host (D2H) copy of their activations over PCIe, a CPU forward pass through those experts (plain GEMMs on AVX-512 or similar), and a host-to-device (H2D) copy of the results. The two streams are then combined (typically a weighted sum) before the next layer.

Speed is throttled by three things. First, **PCIe bandwidth** (~32 GB/s on Gen4 x16) bounds how fast activations can shuttle; for small batches the fixed transfer latency dominates and you're essentially doing a round-trip per token. Second, **CPU compute**: an offloaded expert is a small FFN, but without tensor cores the per-flop latency is 10–50× higher, so the CPU pass itself can become the critical path. Third, **data-dependent control flow**: you can't prefetch "which experts I'll need" until the router fires, so the D2H transfer can't be fully hidden behind other layers' compute. Larger batches amortize the PCIe cost, and aggressive overlap (running CPU experts for layer *i* while the GPU handles layer *i+1*'s router) helps, but the fundamental ceiling is the PCIe link plus the slower CPU FLOPs.

The label encodes the **quantization recipe**, not the model. `Q4_K_M` tells you the per-tensor scheme: a "super-block" K-quant at ~4.835 bpw average, where the "M" variant assigns Q4_K to most tensors, Q5_K to a subset (typically attention V and FFN gate), Q8_0 to a few (e.g., `token_embd` in some builds), and leaves small tensors in f16. `IQ3_XXS` tells you it's an imatrix-guided 3-bit quant (~3.06 bpw) using the XS block structure with specific scale/offset layouts.

What it **doesn't** tell you:

- **Which tensors got which sub-quant.** The "M" is a policy, but exact assignments can shift across llama.cpp versions or forks.
- **Calibration provenance.** IQ variants require an imatrix (per-channel activation statistics). The label doesn't reveal the calibration dataset, sample count, or whether the imatrix was from the same distribution you'll serve.
- **Architecture or size.** `Q4_K_M` on a 7B and a 70B are different files with very different absolute quality.
- **Effective quality.** Same label, different model family, different training run → different perplexity. The label is a *recipe*, not a *score*.
- **Tooling version.** A `Q4_K_M` produced by an older quantize script may differ in edge-case handling from a newer one.

Treat the label as a file-format tag, not a quality guarantee.

## AFM-47 — Non-zero exit from a search command misread as a tool error

**Date:** 2026-09-24

### What happened

The ledger's extractor logged every tool result flagged `is_error` as a bare `ERR <first 120 chars>` line, with no command attached. On this day a compound command—`grep ...; which faketime`—exited 1 because `grep` found no match. That is normal search behavior, not a failure. But the extractor still tagged the result as an error, so the ordinary `grep` output (`argus/driver.py:9: ...route that exists in no Hermes codebase`, an old docstring) was written into the diary skeleton as an `ERR` entry.

A local model then read that entry and fabricated a cause-and-effect narrative linking it to an unrelated change: *"hit a route … Worked around by setting `TZ` and `HERMES_TIMEZONE`."* Neither half of that story was true, and the alleged "workaround" was itself a bug (see the MTP-agentic timezone correction).

### Root cause

Exit status reflects only the **last** command in a compound expression. For search and compare commands (`grep`, `diff`, `cmp`, …) a non-zero exit typically means *nothing matched*, not *something broke*. The extractor conflated the two.

### General lesson

For any tool that summarizes or re-narrates tool output:

1. **Attach the full command and an error class to every `ERR` line before a model is allowed to reason about it.** A bare 120-character snippet is not enough context.
2. **Treat a model-written "why it failed" narrative as an unverified claim**, not as a record. The claim is valid only if it cites the failing call.

### Fix

- Classified `ERR` lines (search-no-match vs. genuine failure).
- Added prompt rules that require the failing call to be cited before any causal explanation is accepted.
- Introduced an inline `_[unverified]_` tagger so fabricated narratives are visibly flagged.

All changes landed in **CHANGELOG 2026-09-24**.

**Discovered by:** a human-requested spot-check of the diary, per the ledger's acceptance criterion (1).

## The core problem: VBR error depends on path, not just state

A static codec's error is determined by its **configuration**. VBR's error is determined by its **history**: which layers were shed, *when* in the sequence, and how many times existing tokens were re-encoded along the way.

This means two runs can end at the same bits/value yet produce different fidelity, depending on when memory pressure hit. A single-shot benchmark cannot tell them apart, because the quantity under test is a trajectory, not a final state.

### Reproducibility is further compromised by the budget source

The VBR budget is derived from **live per-device free memory** (`:1497–1519`). The `VBR_BUDGET_MIB` override exists for testing and is documented as *"forced-budget instrumentation must never grow."* Without that override, **VBR's behaviour changes with whatever else is resident on the GPU.** Co-tenancy is a first-class concern in this code.

### Why `frontier-hazard` cannot see any of this

`frontier-hazard` builds one context, runs a single prefill, scores, and exits. There is no progressive pressure and no re-encode event, so **the mechanism VBR exists to handle never fires.** On top of that, at `--n-prefix 128` the cache occupies only 1–4 MiB against a budget measured in GiB, so the trigger cannot arm even if the env var is set. Taken together with `SCOPE_CORRECTION_136_TOKENS.md`: **VBR is not under-measured by our panels—it is unmeasurable by them.**
